title: What session hijacking means
basic: A session lets an application recognize a user across requests. In a bearer-token design, possession of a valid token can be sufficient to act within that session.
intermediate: Session hijacking is unauthorized use of another user session. It differs from guessing a password, although either can lead to account compromise.
advanced: A login protected by MFA can still issue a bearer session afterward. Evaluate how subsequent requests and sensitive actions are authenticated.
practice: Draw browser, application and session store. Label the credential used for login separately from the session token used afterward.

title: Session lifecycle and trust boundaries
basic: Follow anonymous browsing, login, authenticated requests, privilege changes, logout and expiration.
intermediate: For each transition, record which identifier changes and which server-side permission state is retained.
advanced: A renewed browser cookie does not prove that the previous token was invalidated. Check old and new states against a protected endpoint.
practice: Build a table with transition, old token accepted, new token accepted and expected identity. Use only synthetic lab accounts.

title: Session fixation versus token theft
basic: Fixation involves an identifier known or influenced before a victim authenticates. Token theft involves obtaining an already authenticated credential.
intermediate: Authentication should not elevate a pre-login identifier that remains usable by another party. Rotate the session identifier at the authentication boundary.
advanced: An identifier change alone is insufficient if the former identifier still reaches authenticated state. Check invalidation and identity binding together.
practice: In your own fixture, compare the pre-login identifier with the authenticated identifier and verify the former has no authenticated access.

title: How session credentials become exposed
basic: Exposure can occur through insecure transport, script-accessible storage, accidental logs, URLs or compromised browser components.
intermediate: Inventory token locations without copying real values into reports. Review telemetry, analytics, error messages and debugging exports for accidental disclosure.
advanced: A leaked credential is sensitive even if it looks random or is signed. Signing usually does not make the contents confidential or prevent bearer replay.
practice: Use a clearly fake token in a local logging fixture and verify that logs redact it. Never publish real cookies in screenshots or examples.

title: Cookie controls and their limits
basic: Secure restricts cookie transmission to secure contexts under browser rules. HttpOnly prevents ordinary page JavaScript from reading the cookie.
intermediate: SameSite limits some cross-site cookie sending. Choose scope and attributes according to the application flow; test login redirects and embedded flows.
advanced: HttpOnly does not prevent injected script from issuing actions in the current browser session. Cookie flags do not replace server-side authorization.
practice: Review Set-Cookie in your lab browser developer tools. Record the attributes and purpose while redacting the value.

title: Distinguish hijacking, XSS and CSRF
basic: XSS executes unwanted script in an application context. CSRF induces unwanted authenticated requests from a browser. Neither necessarily requires reading a session token.
intermediate: Keep separate findings for token disclosure, unintended actions and missing object authorization. Their evidence and repairs differ.
advanced: One control may reduce several risks without resolving all of them. Test the specific security property rather than treating any one cookie flag as complete protection.
practice: Write three fictional findings: exposed token, forged state-changing request and another user record returned. Assign the appropriate control to each.

title: Expiration, logout and revocation
basic: A session should stop granting access when its server-enforced validity ends. Closing a browser is not a reliable revocation test.
intermediate: Distinguish idle timeout from absolute lifetime. After logout, check that the former lab credential is rejected by the protected service.
advanced: In distributed systems, caches and replication can delay invalidation. Measure the observed window and compare it with the documented policy.
practice: Record access before logout, immediately afterward and after the expected propagation interval; do not infer access solely from a cached page.

title: Opaque sessions, JWTs and refresh tokens
basic: An opaque session identifier typically references server-side state. A self-contained signed token carries claims that a verifier must validate.
intermediate: Validate issuer, audience, expiry and signature according to the chosen design. A refresh token is a separate credential with its own lifecycle.
advanced: Stateless validation makes immediate revocation a design problem. Refresh rotation can detect reuse only when corresponding state and race handling exist.
practice: Document whether logout revokes server sessions, access tokens, refresh tokens or only clears one browser cookie. Explain any remaining validity window.

title: Detection and incident response
basic: Monitor session creation, renewal, revocation and suspicious use without recording raw tokens.
intermediate: A sudden location or device change can justify investigation or step-up authentication, but is not conclusive evidence of hijacking.
advanced: Mobile networks, shared gateways and privacy tools can change signals. Balance detection with false positives and avoid relying on IP binding as the sole defense.
practice: For a fictional exposed token: revoke affected sessions, investigate the disclosure source, repair it and verify that replacement credentials are protected.

title: Authorized test workflow and reporting
basic: Use an isolated application and two accounts you control. Define the expected session policy before testing.
intermediate: With browser developer tools or Burp Repeater scoped to your own lab, inspect login rotation, logout invalidation, expiry and the identity returned by a protected endpoint.
advanced: Check status, response content and actual server-side identity. A 200 response may be a login page; redirects and caches can disguise denial or success.
practice: Record token labels such as OLD-A and NEW-A instead of values. Report minimal reproduction, affected transition, expected versus observed identity, remediation and retest.
